title: First Nations Invest in Genomics Testing for Their Fisheries | The Tyee
text:
People in B.C. are headed to the polls in October for municipal elections across the province.

At the same time, local newsrooms have been gutted, with existing reporting teams trying to do more with less.

Local politics are hugely consequential for how we live day to day but often have the lowest voter turnouts of any kinds of elections.

The Tyee’s independent journalists are on the ground, tracking candidates and issues across the province.

And we’re asking our readers what is most important to you this civic election season.

That’s because we work for you. Our non-profit newsroom is funded in large part directly by our readers, who we call Tyee Builders. As a Builder, you can contribute an amount that works for you, on your schedule, and help support the public interest journalism that is crucial during the democratic process. And because we’re a registered journalism organization, you’ll get a tax receipt for your contribution over $5.

Every dollar received from our readers ensures our talented team of journalists can get to work and make our reporting available to the public, free of charge, no paywall.

Support good journalism during election season and become a Tyee Builder today.

— Jeanette Ageson, Publisher

You made it all the way to the bottom of the article. That makes you some serious Tyee Builder material.

What’s a Tyee Builder, you ask? It’s a person, a reader, who has decided they want to be part of the team that helps keep open-access, public interest journalism alive.

Without them, without you, the Tyee’s newsroom, staffed with fiercely independent reporters and editors, would not be able to devote all their time to getting to the truth and sharing it freely with the world.

The Tyee is not part of a big news chain or owned by people who are trying to turn a profit. Our non-profit newsroom doesn’t stuff our pages with annoying ads or lock our work behind a paywall. But we still have bills to pay, and good journalism costs a lot. The only way we can square this circle is if a certain percentage of our readers agree to support our newsroom. And luckily, over 10,000 people have decided to do so.

With the help of our readers, we’ve bucked the doom and gloom trend in Canadian media – we’ve grown our team, reach more people than ever, and publish impactful journalism that sparks conversations, reveals truths and moves social change.

Back the team that powers our newsroom – you choose the amount, the frequency, and you can cancel at any time. Plus, you’ll get a tax receipt for your contributions over $5.

If you value the work The Tyee does, please consider becoming a Tyee Builder today.

— Jeanette Ageson, Publisher

A new First Nations salmon genomics project has launched on the west coast of Vancouver Island.

‘Insights’ takes audiences far and wide with stories of struggle, triumph and renewal.

The Ahousaht, Ehattesaht, Mowachaht/Muchalaht, Hesquiaht and Tla-o-qui-aht First Nations are building their capacity for salmon genomics analysis, which will help them manage fisheries and conservation.

Genomics studies DNA sequence, the function of genes and the complexity of their interactions.

It can also be used a bit like an ID check, where a sample of a fish’s adipose fin or tail can be used to estimate where the fish is from.

Currently this ID check is run by Fisheries and Oceans Canada, commonly known as DFO, at its Molecular Genetics Laboratory at the Pacific Biological Station in Nanaimo. The Nanaimo lab has spent decades building a vast library of salmon genomics data from salmon-bearing streams all along the coast.

It can check 550 genetic markers from a sample against this library to figure out where a wild fish is from.

Researchers can pull even more data on hatchery fish, said Ben Sutherland, an adjunct professor at Vancouver Island University and founder of Sutherland Bioinformatics. This data includes information on a fish’s parentage.

“We can actually tell it came from those two parents, the age of the fish, what hatchery released it and any other data about the parents,” he said. “It allows us to track where these individuals came from with a really good resolution.”

The problem is that this single lab in Nanaimo currently does all the genomics testing for the entire coast.

DFO is obliged to process fishery samples and can only process samples from other groups, such as First Nations, once its priorities are met, Candace Picco, senior biologist with Ha’oom Fisheries Society, told The Tyee. This means it can take a long time to get results.

Ha’oom Fisheries Society helps the Ahousaht, Ehattesaht, Mowachaht/Muchalaht, Hesquiaht and Tla-o-qui-aht First Nations implement their commercial rights-based fisheries.

Demand for the DFO lab has been high and wait times have been long since the early 2000s. They worsened earlier this year when DFO cut staff from the genomics lab, said Howie Wight, executive director of the Ha’oom Fisheries Society and member of the Gitxsan Nation.

To cut wait times down to a couple days, the five nations are building their own genomics lab, which will be able to test a smaller number of samples but will provide faster results.

“While the time it takes to get results is really important and we want to shorten that, it’s more about having the power and agency to choose the priority for sample processing,” Picco said.

To do this, Sutherland and Picco are working out how to genotype new fish samples outside of the DFO lab before comparing the results against DFO’s genomics library.

There are two avenues they’re exploring to do this.

The first is using a Nanopore sequencer to do remote genotyping. While this technology has been used reliably in other applications, it’s currently in the research and development stage for the project’s particular needs. If all goes well, it could turn samples around in two to three days.

The second avenue is working with an independent lab to sequence samples. This lab would be able to return results in six to eight weeks.

Ideally in the future Ha’oom will be able to choose if it wants to spend a little more and get speedy results or spend a little less and wait a month or two for results, Sutherland said.

The second part of the project is building analysis software that can compare these results to the DFO library.

The project is called “decentralizing salmonid genetic stock identification with First Nations-led technological innovation and collaboration.”

This is the most comprehensive sharing of DFO’s salmon genomics library outside the organization, Sutherland said.

The project complements the work done by and the resources held by DFO, Picco and Sutherland said.

A stapler-sized sequencer

There are a lot of benefits that will come with using the hand-held Nanopore sequencer.

For starters, it’s a fraction of the size and the cost of a larger sequencer used in the DFO lab.

The Nanopore is around the size of a stapler. It needs to be connected to a laptop and costs under $10,000, Sutherland said. It could be used dockside to test samples.

By comparison, buying a larger sequencer typically costs hundreds of thousands of dollars, needs much more space, needs trained personnel to run and maintain it, can’t be used outside the lab and is typically only cost effective when used on a fairly regular basis with a large volume of samples, he said.

Because the Nanopore is cheaper more groups will be able to buy and use the tech, Picco said.

One downside is that the smaller sequencer can process fewer samples than a larger one can.

A bigger set of samples, such as 500 to 1,000 or more, are best run by a larger sequencer, Sutherland said.

Remote First Nations have a lot of questions that could potentially be answered by this tech, Picco said, such as how to catch all of the hatchery fish to avoid interbreeding with the wild stock and how to avoid inbreeding in hatcheries.

However, the project will still have to show that the Nanopore sequencer creates the same data results as the DFO lab.

A sequencer of any size is just a tool to help humans read the data stored in a genome.

Several different sequencers should produce the same data set from a single sample because the genetic data in that sample didn’t change.

This repeatability is what allows samples to be checked against the DFO library, because, for example, a coho salmon from the Rivers Inlet area caught anywhere on the coast will always produce a dataset similar to other coho salmon from the Rivers Inlet area.

However, the team still hasn’t proven that samples sequenced remotely by the Nanopore consistently produce the same results as the DFO lab does.

If it creates slightly different data then it will be like “apples and oranges” and not able to be checked against DFO’s library, Sutherland said.

The project’s genomics analysis will focus on coho and chinook, which are the two main kinds of salmon harvested on the west coast of Vancouver Island.

When the project is up and running First Nations will also be able to have data sovereignty, meaning they’ll own the data they collect and decide whether or not they want to share it with DFO. That sovereignty is “really important” for First Nations because historically DFO didn’t automatically share its data, Picco said.

Other nations are watching with interest

The seeds of this project stretch back to a court case where the Ahousaht, Ehattesaht, Mowachaht/Muchalaht, Hesquiaht and Tla-o-qui-aht First Nations affirmed their right to run fisheries in their own territories, Picco said. The judge mandated DFO and the nations to work together to manage the fisheries by the nations’ “preferred means,” which has been an ongoing negotiation, she added.

But to run a fishery, a nation needs to know what salmon stocks they’re catching, she said.

Wight said he previously worked with the Okanagan Nation Alliance and DFO as the alliance set up capacity for genomic testing to check their salmon populations for viruses or diseases.

Ha’oom wanted to make that happen on the coast too and secured financial support from the Indigenous Stewardship Fund, the Pacific Salmon Foundation and Genome B.C.

The Indigenous Stewardship Fund is providing $365,000 over three years, which makes up the bulk of the project’s funding.

Many First Nations want access to and control of data about their territories, and this one project offered a portable, scalable solution to that problem, said Yasmin Passos, senior manager for operations at the Indigenous Stewardship Fund.

The Indigenous Stewardship Fund is the charitable arm of the First Nations Fisheries Council, which works with over 200 nations in B.C. to create a common voice.

Many other First Nations are watching the project with interest.

First Nations in the Skeena River basin, the Central Coast, Vancouver Island, the Fraser River and Columbia River systems are keen to build their own genomic analysis capacity if the project works, Wight said.

At the end of the three years Sutherland said he hopes to have Ha’oom scientists trained on most of the processing and analysis of samples; that the Nanopore approach will allow for remote genotyping to be done within a couple of days; and that the new lab is producing the same results as the DFO lab. He also hopes to have access to DFO’s library and good communication between all groups.

On top of that he’s really excited to see what happens when the ability to check genomics is in the hands of First Nations, because when the technology is in the hands of the end-user there’s more creativity in testing what kind of questions the technology can be used to answer, he said.

There’s nothing like a celebration, and on Saturday, Sept. 19, the BC and Yukon Book Prizes celebrated the winners of the 42nd Book Prizes.

This year’s winners included Endling by Maria Reva, We Survived the Night by Julian Brave NoiseCat and Buzzkill Clamshell by Amber Dawn. A total of eight prizes were awarded along with the Lieutenant Governor’s Award for Literary Excellence and the Borealis Prize: The Commissioner of Yukon Award for Literary Contribution.

The award celebrations were punctuated by entertainment that combined unique poetry by local poets including 2017 Dorothy Livesay Poetry Prize winner Adèle Barclay, which was paired with drag performances by Tiffany Ann Co., AndrogynAss and Jaryd.
